units.text: INT. LAMPLIGHTER'S COTTAGE - EARLY MORNING
A one-room cottage with a low beam ceiling and a stove gone cold.
A ladder-pole leans in the corner.
Shelves of oil cans, wicks, brass snuffers.
Gray fog presses against the windowpane.
ARCHIBALD "ARCHIE" PENNYWORTH, seventies, the last lamplighter in the parish, sits in his chair by the dead stove in a coat too large for him.
His hands, big-knuckled, rest on his knees like tools put down.
His granddaughter, CORDELIA PENNYWORTH, nineteen, in a plain gray dress and a new hat, stands in the doorway with a leather satchel, the sound of the city already in her shoulders.
The electric men start Monday.
units.name: CORDELIA

units.text: So I hear.
units.name: ARCHIE

units.text: They say the whole of Harrow Lane will be lit by noon.
units.name: CORDELIA

units.text: By noon.
units.name: ARCHIE

units.text: He picks up a brass snuffer from the shelf and turns it in his fingers.
She crosses to him, kneels, and puts her hand over his.
You can come to the city.
units.name: CORDELIA

units.text: What would I do in a city?
units.name: ARCHIE

units.text: Sit. Watch the lamps come on.
units.name: CORDELIA

units.text: Without me to light them?
units.name: ARCHIE

units.text: She doesn't answer.
He sets the snuffer back on its hook and, with the slow care of a man doing something for the last time, rises and takes the long pole from the corner.
Come along, then. I've one street left.
units.name: ARCHIE
